title: Rip Van Winkle
description: A lazy, good-hearted Dutch villager wanders into the Catskill mountains, drinks with a silent ghostly crew playing ninepins, and wakes twenty years later to a new country that no longer knows him.

cover.alt: A company of odd-looking men in old Dutch dress playing ninepins in a mountain hollow
cover.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The village at the foot of the mountains
elements.text: In an old Dutch village on the Hudson, under King George, lives Rip Van Winkle, loved by children and dogs and scolded by his wife.

metadata.source_quote: Every change of season, every change of weather, indeed, every hour of the day, produces some change in the magical hues and shapes of these mountains

image.alt: Good wives looking up at the Kaatskill mountains to tell the weather
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Petticoat government
elements.text: Rip will help any neighbour but never works his own farm. Dame Van Winkle's tongue drives him out of the house.

metadata.source_quote: a tart temper never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use.

image.alt: Dame Van Winkle scolding at the door, driving Rip out of the house
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The club of sages
elements.text: He hides on the bench outside the inn with Nicholas Vedder and the village wise men, until his wife finds him there too.

image.alt: Village sages gathered on a bench before a small inn under a tree
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: A stranger with a keg
elements.text: Out shooting squirrels with his dog Wolf, Rip hears his name called and helps a short old Dutchman carry a keg up a ravine.

image.alt: Strange beings in the trees of the Catskill mountains, a region full of fable
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Ninepins in the hollow
elements.text: In a mountain amphitheatre men in antique Dutch dress play ninepins in silence; the balls sound like thunder.

metadata.source_quote: On a level spot in the centre was a company of odd-looking personages playing at ninepins.

image.alt: A company of odd-looking men in old Dutch dress playing ninepins in a mountain hollow
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The flagon
elements.text: They stare at him with fixed eyes. He serves their drink, tastes it, then tastes again, and falls asleep.

image.alt: Rip tasting from the flagon among red-capped mushrooms
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Waking
elements.text: He wakes on the green knoll: his gun is rusted, Wolf is gone, and his beard is a foot long.

metadata.source_quote: “Surely,” thought he, “I have not slept here all night.

image.alt: Rip waking under a tree, old and bearded, his gun rusted
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: A strange village
elements.text: Children he does not know follow him hooting, dogs bark at him, his house is a ruin.

image.alt: A troop of children running after Rip, pointing at his grey beard
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The new sign
elements.text: The inn is a hotel, a flagpole stands where the tree was, and King George on the sign has become General Washington. A man harangues about elections.

metadata.source_quote: the ruby face of King George, under which he had smoked so many a peaceful pipe

image.alt: The crowd around Rip outside the inn, eyeing him from head to foot
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Who are you?
elements.text: Accused of being a Tory spy, asked who he is, Rip sees his own double leaning on a tree, and no longer knows.

image.alt: Villagers staring at the stranger and stroking their chins
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Judith
elements.text: A young woman with a baby tells him her father, Rip Van Winkle, went to the mountains twenty years ago. He knows her.

metadata.source_quote: Rip Van Winkle was his name, but it’s twenty years since he went away from home with his gun

image.alt: Rip's daughter holding her child, a black cat at her feet
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The storyteller
elements.text: Old Peter Vanderdonk vouches for the legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew. Rip settles back on the inn bench and tells his tale to every traveller.

metadata.source_quote: He used to tell his story to every stranger that arrived at Mr. Doolittle’s hotel.

image.alt: Old Rip telling his story by the fire to wide-eyed children
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Rip Van Winkle
elements.text: A kind, idle descendant of Dutch settlers, ready to help anyone but himself.

metadata.source_quote: The great error in Rip’s composition was an insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labour.

image.alt: Rip with the village children, who follow him everywhere
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Dame Van Winkle
elements.text: Rip's wife, whose scolding rules the house; she dies while he sleeps.

image.alt: Dame Van Winkle lecturing from behind the bed-curtains while a cat listens
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Wolf
elements.text: Rip's dog, as henpecked as his master, who comes home without him.

image.alt: Dogs barking at Rip as he walks into the village
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Hendrick Hudson's crew
elements.text: The ghostly sailors of the Half-moon who return to the Catskills every twenty years to play ninepins.

metadata.source_quote: with his crew of the Half-moon

image.alt: The strange bearded players, keeping the gravest faces
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Judith Gardenier
elements.text: Rip's grown daughter, who takes him in.

image.alt: Rip's daughter holding her child, a black cat at her feet
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Nicholas Vedder
elements.text: The silent patriarch of the village inn, who answers by how he smokes his pipe.

image.alt: Village sages gathered on a bench before a small inn under a tree
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The Kaatskill mountains
elements.text: Blue-and-purple mountains above the Hudson, changing colour with the weather.

image.alt: Good wives looking up at the Kaatskill mountains to tell the weather
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The village and the inn
elements.text: A little Dutch village of yellow-brick houses with an inn under a great tree, later a hotel under a flagpole.

image.alt: Houses of the original Dutch settlers in the village
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The amphitheatre
elements.text: A hollow ringed by cliffs high in the mountains, where the ghosts play.

image.alt: A company of odd-looking men in old Dutch dress playing ninepins in a mountain hollow
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Twenty years in a night
elements.text: The Catskills keep a magic of their own: a drink that stops time.

image.alt: Rip waking under a tree, old and bearded, his gun rusted
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: The American Revolution
elements.text: The war Rip sleeps through, which turns colonists into citizens and King George into a painted-over sign.

image.alt: The crowd around Rip outside the inn, eyeing him from head to foot
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Identity is held by others
elements.text: When nobody remembers you, it is hard to remember yourself.

image.alt: Villagers staring at the stranger and stroking their chins
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: History happens elsewhere
elements.text: The great events of the nation pass Rip by, and life in the village goes on much as before.

image.alt: The crowd around Rip outside the inn, eyeing him from head to foot
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Idleness forgiven
elements.text: Irving's comedy is gentle: the idler is rewarded with a happy old age and a story to tell.

image.alt: Old Rip telling his story by the fire to wide-eyed children
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: How legends harden
elements.text: Rip's story wavers at first and then settles into the version everybody knows by heart.

metadata.source_quote: He was observed, at first, to vary on some points every time he told it

image.alt: Old Rip telling his story by the fire to wide-eyed children
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.

elements.title: Peter Klaus
elements.text: A German folk tale of a goatherd who sleeps twenty years after watching knights play ninepins in the Kyffhäuser mountains; Irving's source.

elements.title: Diedrich Knickerbocker
elements.text: Irving's invented Dutch historian, to whom the tale is attributed.

elements.title: Henry Hudson
elements.text: The explorer whose ship, the Half Moon, sailed up the Hudson in 1609.

image.alt: The strange bearded players, keeping the gravest faces
image.credit: Arthur Rackham, illustration for Rip Van Winkle (Heinemann, 1905). Public domain.
